title: Lesson 14: Setting Up a Consultancy: Legal, Finance, Tooling, and Operations
description: How a principal builds the legal entity, finances, tooling, and operating rhythm that own and keep alive the assets a practice compounds.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Setting Up a Consultancy: Legal, Finance, Tooling, and Operations”, what is the core reason for forming a legal entity rather than contracting as an individual?
options: To reduce the tax the practice pays on consulting income.
To separate the practice's obligations from the person's, so the company can be liable without the founder losing personal assets.
To make invoicing simpler for enterprise clients.
To allow the practice to hire contractors without a written agreement.
questions.explanation: The lesson says that without an entity every contract, dispute, and judgment lands on the person, and that separation is the whole reason the entity exists.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Setting Up a Consultancy: Legal, Finance, Tooling, and Operations”, why is separating the practice's money from the founder's personal money the first financial act?
options: Because it is required before the practice can file a tax return.
Because mixing the two makes the founder personally liable for business debts.
Because clients will not contract with a practice that pays personal expenses.
Because a practice whose revenue and delivery cost do not land in the same books cannot know what it costs to deliver, so it cannot price.
questions.explanation: The lesson says separation is what makes the operating numbers of utilization, capacity, and margin computable at all.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Setting Up a Consultancy: Legal, Finance, Tooling, and Operations”, what does the lesson say about ownership of the practice's functions?
options: Every function has to have a named owner, so that when a person leaves their functions are already named and can be reassigned.
The principal should own every function until the practice can afford a dedicated operator for it.
Ownership can be implicit as long as the team is small and communicates well.
Only the reference architectures and internal tooling need named owners.
questions.explanation: The lesson says a practice where ownership is implicit is one departure away from discovering it did not actually know how its own firm ran.
